summary: RPID adds optional elements to the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) that give richer information about a presentity and its contacts. Much of it can be derived automatically, for example from calendars. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of only online or offline, your status can say what you are doing, such as in a meeting, on a plane or at lunch.

questions: what does rpid add to pidf
what is the rpid user-input element

subtitle: Optional XML elements that let presence say what a person is doing, where they are and how best to reach them.

tldr.problem: PIDF can only say open or closed plus a contact URI and a human-readable note, which is too little for software to judge whether a communication attempt is appropriate.
tldr.mechanism: RPID adds optional elements for persons, services (tuples) and devices, such as activities, mood, place, privacy and user-input. They are chosen so many can be derived automatically from calendars, devices or sensors.
tldr.outcome: RPID documents stay valid PIDF, so PIDF-only watchers and gateways keep working, just without the extra detail. Because the data can be highly sensitive, systems should let users reveal it selectively.

today: RFC 4480 is a Standards Track (Proposed Standard) document from July 2006, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Beyond Open and Closed
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF, RFC 3863) is an XML format with a <presence> root, <tuple> elements that each carry a contact URI and a basic status of open or closed, and <note> elements. The note is meant for a human reader, so it is a poor place for facts that software needs to interpret.

RPID adds optional elements for that purpose. The presence data model (RFC 4479) describes a presentity (a presence entity) with three kinds of data: services, encoded as <tuple>; devices, as <device>; and persons, as <person>. RPID extends all three.

There are two stated goals: presence at least as rich as common commercial presence systems, to ease a move to systems built on the Common Profile for Instant Messaging, and backward compatibility with PIDF. The RFC makes no assumption about how the data is generated, and notes users are not always diligent about updating status, so it favors sources such as calendars, device status, typing activity and physical presence detectors. RPID keeps the content type application/pidf+xml.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a chat app just shows a green or red dot. RPID lets the dot come with details, like 'at lunch' or 'in a loud place', that a computer can understand.

sections.title: The Elements at a Glance
sections.content:
Some RPID elements describe services, some devices and some the person, so each extends <tuple>, <device> or <person>. The RFC's Table 1 shows where each may appear. The thirteen elements are activities, class, deviceID, mood, place-is, place-type, privacy, relationship, service-class, sphere, status-icon, time-offset and user-input.

Elements marked in the table MAY carry from and until attributes giving the absolute time a value began and the time until which it is expected to be valid. Several elements of the same type can exist, but their time ranges SHOULD NOT overlap. Elements MAY also have an id attribute. The activities, mood and place-type elements can take an <other> element for custom free text.

All of these elements are optional, and a presentity is unlikely to publish all of them at once. The RFC warns that nothing guarantees the information is accurate, since people forget to update calendars or presence settings. The elements live in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:rpid.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a menu of extra labels you can stick on yourself, your apps or your devices. You only use the labels that you want to share.

sections.title: Describing the Person and Their Surroundings
sections.content:
<activities> lists what the person is doing, and a person can do several things at once, such as traveling and having a meal. Values include meeting, away, busy, on-the-phone, sleeping, steering, vacation and permanent-absence. Several, such as meeting, lunch and travel, can often be derived from a calendar. Publishing permanent-absence implies all services report CLOSED.

<mood> takes one or more child elements such as <happy/> or <sleepy/>, optionally with a <note>. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to support the values from Jabber JEP-0107.

<place-is> describes the surroundings per media type: audio (noisy, ok, quiet), video (toobright, ok, dark) and text (uncomfortable, inappropriate, ok). <place-type> names the kind of place, with its initial values in RFC 4589. <sphere> gives the person's current role, with only work, home and unknown defined. It lets rules switch groups of watchers on or off, as in the RFC's Boy Scout leader example.

<time-offset> is the number of minutes from UTC, positive when east of UTC and negative when west of it. Publishers on mobile devices SHOULD NOT publish it unless it reflects the current location.
sections.plainLanguage: These labels say what you are doing, how you feel, how loud or dark it is where you are, and what time it is for you, so friends know when it is a good time to call.

sections.title: Describing Services and Devices
sections.content:
<class> is a label chosen by the presentity to group similar persons, devices or services, and is generally not shown to the watcher. Each can have only one class. <deviceID> in a tuple refers to the device that provides the service, and one service may use several devices.

<relationship> marks a tuple that refers to someone other than the presentity, such as family, friend, associate, assistant or supervisor. The default is self, and the contact URI then belongs to that other person. <service-class> says how a service is delivered: electronic (the default when omitted), postal, courier, freight, in-person or unknown. The non-electronic types MUST NOT be used unless the contact URI is empty.

<privacy> says which kinds of communication (audio, text, video) bystanders are unlikely to overhear or see. It does not describe the security of the network channel or encryption.

<status-icon> holds a URI of an image. Presentities SHOULD supply suitably sized images, and support for JPEG, PNG and GIF is RECOMMENDED. Watchers MUST check whether their local copy is current using the retrieval protocol's cache control.

<user-input> is either active or idle, with an optional last-input time and an idle-threshold in seconds. A two-state model avoids sending repeated updates during continuous activity. Configuration MUST include the option to omit last-input.
sections.plainLanguage: These labels describe the ways to reach you: which phone or mailbox, whether it is your own or your assistant's, a picture to show, and whether anyone has touched the keyboard lately.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example document is for the presentity pres:someone@example.com. It has tuples for an instant-messaging contact, an assistant's email address marked with <rpid:assistant/>, and an email service with a <status-icon>. It also has a <dm:device> whose user-input is idle with an idle-threshold of 600, and a <dm:person> carrying activities, mood, place-is, place-type, privacy, sphere, status-icon and time-offset.

Each RPID element is qualified with the rpid: prefix, and it sits inside the PIDF or data-model element it extends.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is one big status card with a few entries for each of the person, the devices and the ways to reach them.

sections.title: Extending RPID
sections.content:
Anyone may introduce their own elements by choosing a namespace URI that avoids conflicts. New standardized values for <activities>, <mood>, <privacy>, <relationship> and <service-class> follow the PIDF extension process, with namespace designators like urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:ext. New <place-type> values are assigned by RFC 4589.

To avoid one namespace per element, registrations for one enumeration, such as <privacy>, SHOULD be bundled into a single namespace. Section 7 of the RFC handles the IANA registration of the RPID namespace and schema.
sections.plainLanguage: If the built-in labels are not enough, you can add your own, as long as you give them a unique name so they do not clash with anyone else's.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The security considerations of PIDF (RFC 3863) and the SIP presence event package (RFC 3856) apply. RPID reveals more about a presentity than PIDF, and the information can be highly sensitive. Beyond confidentiality and integrity, systems should let users reveal information selectively to particular watchers and inspect what is published, especially when generated automatically from calendars or sensors.

A <status-icon> is a reference to an external object, so it may induce the watcher to fetch data from a third party (a content indirection attack), retrieving harmful content or adding load to the referenced resource.

On internationalization, RPID mostly uses tokens for programs to translate into the watcher's language. Free-text <note> and <other> elements SHOULD carry an xml:lang attribute, and UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED where encoding support is incompatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing so much about yourself can be risky, so you should choose who sees what. A picture link could also trick someone's app into loading something bad.
